lesson.title: The Map in Your Head: How Rats, and People, Learn Space
lesson.summary: Edward Tolman proposed that animals build internal mental representations of their surroundings, called cognitive maps, challenging the idea that learning is nothing more than a chain of stimulus-response habits.
lesson.body:
You just saw how Bandura's social learning theory argued that behaviorism's strict focus on directly reinforced stimulus-response links couldn't fully explain how people learn, that something more like attention, memory, and expectation had to be happening internally. Decades earlier, working with rats rather than children, Edward Tolman had already been building a related case, and cognitive maps were his central piece of evidence.

The traditional behaviorist account of maze learning treated it as a chain of habits: turn left at this junction because that specific turn, at that specific point, had previously been reinforced. Tolman argued this couldn't be the whole story. He proposed instead that animals form a cognitive map, an internal mental representation of the overall spatial layout of an environment, including how locations relate to one another, not just a memorized sequence of turns.

The evidence came from rats that kept navigating efficiently even when a maze was changed in ways that a pure habit chain shouldn't survive: rats that had learned a maze from one starting point could still find the goal efficiently from a new, never-used starting point, and rats faced with a blocked familiar path would often take the next-shortest available route toward the goal rather than behaving as if they had no idea where to go. That kind of flexible, shortcut-taking navigation is very hard to explain if all the rat has is a rigid sequence of reinforced turns, but it makes sense if the rat has something more like an internal map it can read from any starting point.

The idea generalizes easily to human experience. Anyone who has confidently rerouted around a closed street in a familiar city, or cut through a shortcut they'd never technically walked as a full connected path before, is drawing on something like a cognitive map rather than a memorized list of directions. Cognitive maps set up the next major piece of Tolman's work: if animals are building this kind of internal representation, that learning ought to be detectable even in situations with no reward at all, which is exactly what latent learning demonstrates.
